issues.display_title: Issue #85: Task 1: Session Management Foundation (NextAuth)
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 1: Session Management Foundation (NextAuth)

Context

The app has pages and a working UI but no real memory of who is signed in. Each page load starts fresh — there is no system yet to keep a user logged in across navigation or page refreshes. This task lays the foundation everything else depends on.

Goal

Install and configure the authentication session system so the app knows who is signed in, remembers them across page refreshes, and carries the information needed to talk to the backend on their behalf.

What We're Building

NextAuth is the library that manages user sessions. When a user logs in, NextAuth receives their identity from the backend, encrypts it into a secure cookie stored in their browser, and makes it available to every page in the app.

We configure NextAuth to use email and password credentials. When someone tries to sign in, NextAuth sends those credentials to the GoThru backend, which checks them and returns the user's details along with an access token. NextAuth stores that token inside the session so it can be used for future requests — the user's browser never sees the raw token.

We also extend the session to hold three extra pieces of information: the user's unique ID, whether their email address has been verified, and the access token itself. These are needed by nearly every part of the app that follows.

Why It Matters

Without a session system, the app has no persistent identity for a logged-in user. There is no way to protect pages, no way to show personalised content, and no way to make secure calls to the backend. Every other task in this plan depends on the session being in place.

Acceptance Criteria

  • A user who signs in stays signed in when they refresh the page or open a new tab
  • The session holds the user's ID, name, email, email-verified status, and access token
  • The session is encrypted — inspecting browser cookies does not reveal readable user data
  • If the session is missing or expired, protected pages redirect the user to the login page
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

The app gains memory. Any page or function can now ask "is someone signed in, and if so, who?" and receive a reliable, secure answer.

issues.display_title: Issue #86: Task 2: Authentication Operations (Auth Server Actions)
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 2: Authentication Operations (Auth Server Actions)

Context

Task 1 installed the session system so the app can remember who is signed in. Now we need the actual functions that handle every authentication operation — logging in, registering, verifying an email address, resetting a password. These functions are the bridge between the auth pages and the backend.

Goal

Create a set of secure, server-side functions that handle every authentication operation by talking to the GoThru backend, so that auth pages have clean, reliable operations to call.

What We're Building

Seven behind-the-scenes functions, each responsible for one auth operation:

Login sends the user's email and password to the backend. If correct, it stores the returned session. If the email isn't verified yet, it returns a specific signal so the login page can redirect to the right place.

Register creates a new account on the backend, then immediately signs the user in so they don't have to log in separately after registering.

Verify email sends the one-time token (from the email link) to the backend. The backend confirms it and marks the account as verified.

Resend verification asks the backend to send a fresh verification email. It respects rate limits — if the user requests too many in a short time, it returns a specific message so the page can show a wait period.

Forgot password sends the user's email to the backend to trigger a reset email. It always returns "email sent" regardless of whether the address exists in the system, to protect user privacy.

Validate reset token checks whether a password-reset link is still valid before showing the user the reset form.

Reset password submits the new password along with the reset token to the backend.

All of these run on the server — the browser never sees the raw backend responses or API addresses.

Why It Matters

Without these functions, every auth page would need its own direct backend call from the browser, duplicating error handling, exposing API URLs, and making the session harder to manage. Centralising them here means one change fixes all pages at once.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Logging in with correct credentials creates a session and the user is considered signed in
  • Logging in with wrong credentials returns an error message without exposing backend details
  • Registering creates an account and signs the user in immediately
  • Requesting a password reset always returns "email sent" whether or not the address is registered
  • Resending verification too many times triggers a rate-limit message
  • Each function handles errors gracefully with plain-language messages

What Changes After This Task

Auth operations exist as clean, reusable functions. The login page, register page, forgot password page, and reset password page can now each call a single function without duplicating logic or handling raw backend responses.

issues.display_title: Issue #87: Task 3: Project Data Operations (Project Server Actions)
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 3: Project Data Operations (Project Server Actions)

Context

Tasks 1 and 2 handle the authentication layer — signing in, session management, and email verification. Now we need the equivalent layer for project data: functions that let pages create, read, update, and delete projects, and that talk to the backend securely on the user's behalf.

Goal

Create server-side functions for all project operations so every page that touches project data has a single, consistent, secure way to do it.

What We're Building

Eight behind-the-scenes functions covering everything the app needs to do with projects and files:

List projects fetches all of the signed-in user's projects from the database and returns them ready to display.

Create project starts a new project with optional name and location data, and returns the new project's ID.

Get project fetches the full details of a single project by its ID.

Update project saves changes to a project — this includes the project name, floor configuration, the AI-generated 3D model, the canvas editing state, and the status. This one function is called by the wizard, the editor, and anywhere else that needs to save project data.

Delete project permanently removes a project from the database.

Publish project and Unpublish project control whether a project is publicly visible.

Get current user fetches the signed-in user's profile — name, email, and whether their email is verified.

Delete file removes an uploaded floor plan file linked to a project.

After any operation that changes the project list, the dashboard is automatically marked as needing a refresh so the user always sees up-to-date data.

Why It Matters

Without these functions, every page that needs project data would make its own raw backend call from the browser, each one needing to handle auth headers, errors, and response parsing separately. Centralising this means the dashboard, wizard, and editor all work the same way, and a backend change only needs to be made in one place.

Acceptance Criteria

  • The dashboard can fetch and display all the user's projects
  • Creating a project from the wizard saves it to the database and returns its ID
  • Renaming a project updates it in the database immediately
  • Deleting a project removes it; the dashboard reflects the change
  • Published and unpublished status toggles work correctly
  • Calls made without a valid session fail with an authentication error rather than reaching the backend
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

Any part of the app — the dashboard, the wizard, the editor — can manage project data by importing the right function. No backend URL, no auth header handling, no response parsing needed at the page level.

issues.display_title: Issue #88: Task 4: Page Access Control (Middleware)
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 4: Page Access Control (Middleware)

Context

Tasks 1–3 set up the session system and all the server-side data functions. But nothing yet stops an unauthenticated visitor from typing /dashboard or /editor directly into their browser and seeing whatever the page renders. This task adds the gatekeeper.

Goal

Automatically redirect users to the correct page based on whether they are signed in and whether their email address is verified, before any protected page loads.

What We're Building

A piece of logic that runs before every protected page — the dashboard, the project wizard, and the editor. It checks two things in sequence:

Is the user signed in? If not, they are redirected to the login page. The URL they were trying to reach is preserved in the redirect so they can be sent there after signing in.

Is the user's email verified? If not, and they are trying to reach the project wizard or the editor, they are redirected to the email verification pending page. The dashboard is an exception — unverified users can still reach the dashboard so they can resend the verification email without being locked out entirely.

This logic runs at the network level, before the page even begins to load, so there is no flash of protected content.

Why It Matters

Without this, the only thing stopping someone from accessing protected pages is whether the page itself happens to check for a session. That is fragile — pages get built without always remembering to add that check. Middleware enforces access control in one place for all protected pages at once.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Visiting /dashboard without being signed in redirects to /login
  • Visiting /start or /editor without being signed in redirects to /login
  • Visiting /start or /editor while signed in but with an unverified email redirects to the verification pending page
  • Visiting /dashboard while signed in with an unverified email is allowed (so the user can resend the verification link)
  • Signed-in users with a verified email can access all protected pages without any redirect
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

Protected pages are actually protected. Users are automatically guided to the right place based on their sign-in state, and no protected content is visible to people who should not see it.

issues.display_title: Issue #89: Task 5: Secure File Upload Handler
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 5: Secure File Upload Handler

Context

Tasks 1–4 cover session management, data operations, and page protection. File uploads need separate treatment. Unlike text data (project names, floor configs), actual file bytes cannot travel through the same server functions. They need their own dedicated path — and that path still needs to verify the user is signed in before accepting anything.

Goal

Create a dedicated upload endpoint on the GoThru website server that securely receives floor plan files from the browser and forwards them to the backend storage service with the user's authentication.

What We're Building

A bridge for file uploads. The flow works like this:

  1. The user selects a floor plan image or PDF in the wizard
  2. The browser sends the file to /api/upload — a GoThru website endpoint, not the backend directly
  3. The GoThru website server checks the session to confirm the user is signed in
  4. It attaches the user's access token to the request and forwards the file to the Go backend storage service
  5. The backend saves the file and responds with the stored file path
  6. The website server passes that path back to the browser

The user never communicates with the storage backend directly, and their access token never leaves the server.

Why It Matters

Files cannot be sent through the same server-side functions used for text data — the browser has to initiate the upload directly because of how multipart file data works. But the browser also cannot include the auth token because that token only exists server-side. This dedicated handler solves both problems at once.

Acceptance Criteria

  • A signed-in user can successfully upload a floor plan file from the wizard
  • A request without a valid session returns a 401 error — the file is rejected
  • A request missing the file or the project ID returns a clear error message
  • The file is stored by the backend and the response includes its saved path
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

Users can upload floor plan files. The upload is secure, properly authenticated, and correctly linked to the project being worked on.

issues.display_title: Issue #90: Task 6: Auth Pages Wired to Server Actions
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 6: Auth Pages Wired to Server Actions

Context

Tasks 1–5 built the infrastructure: the session system, the auth functions, the data functions, the upload handler, and the access gatekeeper. The six auth pages (login, register, verify email pending, verify email, forgot password, reset password) currently use old direct backend calls that bypass all of that. This task replaces those calls with the proper server functions from Task 2.

Goal

Update all six authentication pages to use the server actions created in Task 2, so every auth flow works correctly end-to-end with proper session integration and consistent error handling.

What We're Building

Updates to six pages, each connected to its server action:

Login page calls the login action. On success, it redirects to the dashboard. If the backend signals the email is not verified, it redirects to the verification pending page instead. Errors are shown inline.

Register page calls the register action. On success, it redirects to the email verification pending page so the user knows to check their inbox.

Verify email pending page shows the user's masked email address (e.g. j***@gmail.com) and a button to resend the verification email. If they resend too many times, a cooldown timer is shown. There is also a sign-out option for users who registered with the wrong email.

Verify email page is where users land after clicking the link in their verification email. It calls the verify action, and — crucially — immediately refreshes the NextAuth session so the rest of the app knows the email is now verified. The user does not need to log out and back in.

Forgot password page shows an email field. After submitting, it always shows "email sent" regardless of whether the address is in the system, protecting user privacy.

Reset password page first validates the reset token from the link. If valid, it shows the new password form. On success, it confirms the password has been changed.

Why It Matters

The old pages had raw API calls that bypassed the session system, used inconsistent error handling, and checked for email verification through an unreliable cookie. Replacing them with server actions means the session is always the source of truth, errors are handled uniformly, and the auth flow works as the rest of the app expects.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Logging in with correct credentials redirects to /dashboard
  • Logging in with wrong credentials shows an inline error
  • Logging in with an unverified email redirects to /verify-email-pending
  • Registering successfully redirects to /verify-email-pending
  • Verifying email via link updates the session immediately — emailVerified becomes true without requiring re-login
  • Forgot password always shows "email sent" regardless of whether the email is registered
  • The reset password form only shows if the reset token is still valid
  • All pages show appropriate loading and error states
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

All six authentication pages work end-to-end. A new user can register, receive a verification email, verify their account, and be taken to the app — all in one uninterrupted flow. Password reset works. The session is the single source of truth throughout.

issues.display_title: Issue #91: Task 7: Dashboard Page Updated to Use Server Actions
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 7: Dashboard Page Updated to Use Server Actions

Context

Task 6 updated the six auth pages. The dashboard page also has old direct backend calls and checks an outdated cookie to determine whether the user's email is verified. This task updates it to use the proper server functions and the session as the source of truth.

Goal

Update the dashboard to load the user's profile and project list through server actions, and use the session — not a cookie — to determine what banners and options to show.

What We're Building

Updates to the main dashboard page — the first screen users see after logging in.

On load, the dashboard fetches two things at once: the signed-in user's profile (name, email, verification status) and their full project list. Both come through the server actions created in Task 3.

Project management: Renaming a project calls the update server action. Deleting calls the delete action. Both update the on-screen list immediately so the user sees the result without a full page reload.

Email verification banner: If the user's email is not yet verified, an amber banner appears at the top of the dashboard. It reads "Please verify your email" with a "Resend email" button. This banner uses session.user.emailVerified from the NextAuth session — not a cookie — which means it reflects the real, up-to-date state. Clicking resend triggers a 30-second cooldown so the button cannot be spam-clicked.

Logout: The logout option clears the locally stored project ID from the browser, signs the user out of their session, and redirects to the login page.

Why It Matters

The old dashboard called the backend directly from the browser and checked a custom cookie (gf_verified) to detect email verification state. That cookie could become stale or be missing, causing the banner to show incorrectly. Replacing it with the session means the verification state is always accurate and consistent with the rest of the app.

Acceptance Criteria

  • The dashboard loads and displays all the user's projects on arrival
  • Renaming a project updates the list immediately
  • Deleting a project removes it from the list immediately
  • The email verification banner appears for unverified users and is not shown for verified users
  • Clicking "Resend email" on the banner works and shows a 30-second cooldown
  • Logging out clears the session and redirects to /login
  • If loading fails (e.g. session expired), the user is redirected to /login
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

The dashboard is fully functional with real data. Users can see all their projects, manage them, and act on their account status — all from one place.

issues.display_title: Issue #92: Task 8: Logout Button Component
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 8: Logout Button Component

Context

Task 7 added logout to the dashboard. The editor also has a logout button in its top bar, and potentially other places in the app will need one too. Rather than duplicating the logout logic in each location, this task creates a single reusable component that can be placed anywhere.

Goal

Create a reusable logout button that properly signs the user out, cleans up locally stored data, and redirects them to the login page.

What We're Building

A single button component — "Sign out" — that can be dropped into any page. When clicked, it does three things in sequence:

  1. Removes the locally stored project ID from the browser (so it does not appear to a different user who signs in later on the same device)
  2. Signs the user out of their NextAuth session, clearing the session cookie
  3. Redirects the user to the login page

While the sign-out is in progress, the button shows "Signing out…" and is disabled to prevent double-clicks.

The component is used in the editor's top bar and can be added to the dashboard header or anywhere else a sign-out option is needed.

Why It Matters

Without a dedicated component, each page that needs a logout button would need to duplicate the logic: clear local storage, call sign out, redirect. If the logout behaviour ever needs to change (e.g., additional cleanup), it would need to be updated in multiple places. A shared component means one update covers everywhere.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Clicking the button signs the user out and redirects them to /login
  • The locally stored project ID is removed before the redirect
  • The button shows "Signing out…" and is unclickable while the sign-out is in progress
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

The editor and dashboard both have a working, consistent logout button. Any future page that needs sign-out can use the same component without additional work.

issues.display_title: Issue #93: Task 9: Project ID and Save Status in the App Store
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 9: Project ID and Save Status in the App Store

Context

The app uses a central store (Zustand) to hold shared state — things like the current map view, layers, and UI settings. To support saving and auto-saving in the wizard and editor (Tasks 10 and 11), the store needs to know which project is currently open and what state the save is in. This task adds those fields.

Goal

Add project tracking and save status fields to the central app store so that the wizard, editor, and any other part of the app can share a consistent view of the current project and saving state.

What We're Building

Three new pieces of shared state, plus the actions to update them:

Current project ID — the database ID of the project the user is currently working on. When set, it is also written to the browser's local storage so it survives a page refresh. When cleared, it is removed from local storage. This is what lets the wizard and editor know which project to save data to.

Saving indicator — a true/false flag that is set to true when a save is in progress and false when it completes. The editor toolbar reads this to show "Saving…" while work is being saved.

Last saved timestamp — the exact time of the most recent successful save. The editor toolbar reads this to show "Last saved 2 minutes ago" (or similar) so the user knows their work is up to date.

Why It Matters

Without these in the central store, the wizard and editor would each need to manage their own copies of the current project ID and save state. They would risk getting out of sync — for example, the editor might not know which project to save to after the wizard created it.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Setting the project ID stores it in local storage and makes it readable from the store
  • Clearing the project ID removes it from local storage
  • The saving flag can be toggled true/false and read by any component
  • The last-saved timestamp can be updated and read by any component
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

The app has a reliable, shared source of truth for the current project and save status. The wizard (Task 10) and editor (Task 11) can use these fields to coordinate saving without duplicating state.

issues.display_title: Issue #94: Task 10: Wizard Saves Progress at Every Step
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 10: Wizard Saves Progress at Every Step

Context

Task 9 added project ID and save state to the central store. The project creation wizard walks users through multiple steps — naming the space, setting the location, configuring floors, and running the AI scan. Currently none of these steps save anything to the database. If the user refreshes the page at any point, all their work is lost. This task fixes that.

Goal

Replace all direct backend calls in the wizard with proper server actions, and save project data to the database at each key step so that progress is preserved through page refreshes.

What We're Building

Updates to the wizard's persistence logic, with saves triggered at the right moments:

Step 1 confirmed (name and location): As soon as the user confirms the project name and location, a project is created in the database. Its ID is stored in the app store and in local storage. From this point forward, all subsequent saves know exactly which project to update.

Floor configuration saved (Step 3 → Step 4): When the user finishes configuring their floors, those settings are saved to the project in the database.

AI scan complete: When the scanning process finishes, the generated 3D model data is saved to the project and the project status is updated to "scanned."

Page restored on load: When the wizard page loads, it checks local storage for a saved project ID. If found, it fetches that project from the database and restores the wizard to the correct step with the saved data.

File uploads still go through the browser-to-server upload path (Task 5) — this is unchanged. File delete operations are now routed through a server action.

Why It Matters

Without persistence, any interruption — a refresh, a closed tab, a browser crash — would mean starting the entire wizard from scratch. For users uploading floor plans and running scans, losing that progress is a significant frustration.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Completing Step 1 creates a project in the database and stores its ID
  • Refreshing mid-wizard restores the user to the correct step with previously saved data
  • Floor configuration data is saved when moving from Step 3 to Step 4
  • AI scan output is saved and the project status changes to "scanned" when complete
  • File uploads remain functional and are linked to the correct project
  • File deletion works and is linked to the correct project
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

The wizard saves progress automatically at each key step. Users can refresh, close the tab, and return later — the wizard picks up where they left off.

issues.display_title: Issue #95: Task 11: Auto-Save and Manual Save in the Editor
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 11: Auto-Save and Manual Save in the Editor

Context

Task 10 handles saving during the creation wizard. Once a project is open in the editor, the user continues making changes — adjusting walls, adding labels, editing the 3D view. Those changes need to be saved too. The editor currently has no save mechanism connected to the backend.

Goal

Add both a manual save button and automatic background saving to the editor, so users never lose their editing work.

What We're Building

Two save mechanisms in the editor toolbar:

Auto-save: Two seconds after the user stops making changes to the canvas, the editor automatically saves the current state to the database in the background. The two-second delay means it does not save on every single drag or click — only after a brief pause. If the network is unavailable when an auto-save triggers, the canvas data is kept in the browser's local storage as a fallback so nothing is lost.

Manual save: A save button in the toolbar that the user can click at any time to save immediately, without waiting for the auto-save delay.

Save status display: The toolbar shows "Saving…" while a save is in progress. Once complete, it shows "Saved [time]" (for example, "Saved just now" or "Saved 3 minutes ago") so the user always knows when their work was last safely stored.

The save operation calls the update project server action from Task 3, storing the full canvas state and marking the project status as "edited."

Why It Matters

Without auto-save, a user who forgets to click save — or whose browser crashes or network drops — loses everything since their last manual save. The combination of auto-save and a fallback to local storage means work is practically never lost.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Making changes and pausing for 2 seconds triggers an automatic save
  • Clicking the save button saves immediately
  • The toolbar shows "Saving…" while saving is in progress
  • The toolbar shows a "Saved [time]" message after each successful save
  • If the network fails during an auto-save, the canvas data is preserved in local storage
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

The editor automatically preserves work without the user needing to remember to save. Changes made in the editor are reflected in the database and survive page refreshes.

Docs

Task 12: Remove Old Proxy Routing Configuration

Context

Before the server actions approach was adopted, the app used a workaround: a configuration rule that forwarded browser requests from /api/v1/* on the GoThru website directly to the Go backend. Now that all backend calls go through server actions (which run server-to-server), this proxy rule is no longer needed. Leaving it in place is misleading and creates a path that could be accidentally used.

Goal

Remove the proxy rewrite configuration from the Next.js config so the codebase accurately reflects how the app actually works.

What We're Building

A cleanup of one configuration file (next.config.ts). The proxy block that forwarded /api/v1/* requests to the backend is removed entirely.

This is a housekeeping task with no visible effect on users — it does not change any behaviour the user can see or interact with. Its value is in keeping the codebase honest and preventing future confusion.

Why It Matters

Leaving unused configuration in place sends the wrong signal to anyone reading the code later. It suggests the browser can still call the backend directly through /api/v1/* — which it should no longer be able to do. It also creates a surface that could accidentally be used, bypassing the server-action security model. Removing it makes the architecture match reality.

Acceptance Criteria

  • The next.config.ts file no longer contains any proxy rewrite block for /api/v1/*
  • The app builds cleanly with no errors
  • No existing functionality is broken — all pages and features that were working before this task still work after it

What Changes After This Task

The configuration file accurately reflects how the app works. There are no unused or misleading routing rules, and the codebase is cleaner and easier to understand.

Tasks 1–12 cover every piece of the frontend auth and persistence plan. Each task was verified individually as it was built. This final task confirms the whole system works together correctly — that nothing was missed, no old patterns remain, and every user flow passes end-to-end.

What We're Building

A two-part verification pass:

Code audit: A systematic search of the codebase for any remaining instances of old patterns — direct calls to /api/v1/, old API helper functions (apiFetch, apiJSON), and old authentication cookie checks (gf_verified, gf_token). None of these should appear in any browser-side file after Tasks 1–12.

issues.display_title: Issue #98: Task 14: Billing Data Operations (Billing Server Actions)
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 14: Billing Data Operations (Billing Server Actions)

Context

Tasks 1–13 cover authentication, project management, and the editor. This task begins the billing layer. Before any billing pages can be built, we need the underlying functions that talk to the GoThru backend's billing endpoints — the same pattern used in Tasks 2 and 3 for auth and project operations.

Goal

Create three server-side billing functions: one to start a subscription checkout, one to open the billing management portal, and one to check the current subscription status.

What We're Building

Three behind-the-scenes functions, each calling a specific billing endpoint on the Go backend:

Start checkout asks the backend to create a Stripe Checkout Session. The backend creates a customer record in Stripe (if one does not exist yet), sets up a subscription checkout, and returns a URL pointing to Stripe's hosted payment page. The billing page uses this URL to redirect the user to Stripe.

Open billing portal asks the backend for a link to the Stripe Billing Portal — Stripe's hosted interface where existing subscribers can update their payment method, view invoices, or cancel their subscription. The backend looks up the user's Stripe customer record and returns the portal URL.

Get billing status fetches the user's current subscription state from the backend. The possible states are: active (subscription is in good standing), inactive (no subscription), past due (payment failed, Stripe is retrying), and canceled (the user has canceled). It also returns the renewal date for active subscriptions.

All three functions run on the server. If the user is not signed in, they return a safe error or default state without reaching the backend.

Why It Matters

Without these functions, the billing page would need to call the backend directly from the browser, handling auth headers and errors at the page level. Keeping them server-side maintains the same architecture used throughout the rest of the plan and ensures billing API calls are never made directly from the browser.

Acceptance Criteria

  • A signed-in user can call the checkout function and receive a valid Stripe checkout URL
  • A signed-in user with an existing subscription can call the portal function and receive a valid Stripe portal URL
  • The billing status function returns the correct status for a user with no subscription (inactive) and for a user with an active subscription
  • Calling any of the three functions without a valid session returns a safe fallback or error, not an exception
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

The billing data layer exists. The billing pages in Task 15 can import these functions and focus purely on presenting the information and handling user interaction.

issues.display_title: Issue #99: Task 15: Billing Pages (Subscribe, Success, Cancel)
issues.main_description_html:
Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-frontend-auth-plan.md

Task 15: Billing Pages (Subscribe, Success, Cancel)

Context

Task 14 created the three billing server functions. This task builds the three pages users interact with during the billing flow. All payment handling is done by Stripe on their own hosted pages — GoThru only needs to send users there and handle the return.

Goal

Build the main billing page, the payment success page, and the payment cancel page, so users can subscribe to GoThru, manage their plan, and be handled gracefully after completing or abandoning a Stripe checkout.

What We're Building

Three pages:

Billing page (/billing) is the user's subscription hub. When it loads, it fetches the current subscription status from Task 14's status function. Based on what it finds, it shows one of two views:

  • No active subscription: A short message explaining they do not have an active plan, and a "Subscribe" button. Clicking it calls the checkout function, receives the Stripe checkout URL, and immediately redirects the browser to Stripe's payment page.
  • Active subscription: A confirmation that their subscription is active, the renewal date, and a "Manage subscription" button. Clicking it calls the portal function and redirects to the Stripe Billing Portal.

If the subscription is past due or canceled, the appropriate message is shown with a Subscribe button to resume.

Payment success page (/billing/success) is where Stripe redirects the user after a successful payment. It shows a brief "Payment successful — your subscription is now active" confirmation message, then automatically redirects to the dashboard after 3 seconds. No manual action is required from the user.

Payment cancel page (/billing/cancel) is where Stripe redirects the user if they exit the checkout process without paying. It clearly states that no charge was made, and offers a button to go back to the billing page.

Why It Matters

Without these pages, there is no way for users to start or manage a GoThru subscription. The success and cancel pages are required by Stripe — every checkout flow must define where to send the user afterwards.

Acceptance Criteria

  • The billing page loads and shows the correct subscription status
  • Users with no active subscription see a Subscribe button that redirects to Stripe checkout
  • Users with an active subscription see their renewal date and a Manage button that opens the Stripe Billing Portal
  • After a successful Stripe payment, the user lands on /billing/success with a confirmation message and is redirected to the dashboard after 3 seconds
  • After canceling out of Stripe checkout, the user lands on /billing/cancel with a clear message that no charge was made, and a link back to /billing
  • Error states (e.g. failing to create a checkout session) show a plain-language message rather than crashing the page
  • No TypeScript errors

What Changes After This Task

Users can subscribe to GoThru, manage their plan, and view their subscription status. The full billing flow — from the billing page through Stripe checkout and back — works end-to-end.

issues.display_title: Issue #129: Establish the Subtle Hover Colour Values
issues.main_description_html:
Establish the Subtle Hover Colour Values

Docs

Spec

2026-06-22-hover-area-label-design.md

Plan

2026-06-22-hover-area-label.md

Context

The app currently uses a single vivid blue when highlighting a room on hover. That colour works for the selection state (clicking a room) but is too strong for a gentle hover interaction — especially in the public-facing preview where the intent is to feel subtle and welcoming rather than sharp and tool-like.

Before any view-mode logic can be wired up, the two new colour values need to exist as named constants that the rest of the code can reference by name.

Goal

Define a very light blue-grey colour and its matching transparency level as named values, so that every part of the system that needs a subtle hover effect can use the same consistent shade without anyone hard-coding a colour string.

What We're Building

Two new named values added to the file that holds all the map colour definitions:

  • A subtle hover fill colour — a very light blue-grey (#e8f0fe), the same quiet tone used by Mappedin's hover style.
  • A subtle hover opacity — 0.18, just enough to register as interactive without drawing the eye.

These sit alongside the existing colour constants (wall colour, area background, selection outline, etc.) and are exported so the layer rendering system can import and use them.

Why It Matters

Colour decisions made in one place are easy to tune and impossible to get out of sync. If the preview hover colour ever needs to change — say, to match a new brand palette — one edit here updates every consumer automatically. Hard-coding the same hex string in three places would mean hunting for all of them later.

Acceptance Criteria

  • The two new colour constants exist and are exported from the colour definitions file
  • No existing colour constants are changed or removed
  • The codebase builds and typechecks with zero new errors
  • The change is committed on its own so the colour decision is independently traceable

What Changes After This Task

The subtle hover colours are available for Task 2 to import and apply to the hover highlight layer.

RESULT

Added HOVER_FILL_COLOR_SUBTLE and HOVER_FILL_OPACITY_SUBTLE to src/lib/map/layer-definitions.ts, exported for the per-mode room-layer hover paint. Values later tuned by the product owner. No existing constants changed.

issues.display_title: Issue #130: Teach the Room Layer How to Behave Per Mode
issues.main_description_html:
Teach the Room Layer How to Behave Per Mode

Docs

Spec

2026-06-22-hover-area-label-design.md

Plan

2026-06-22-hover-area-label.md

Context

The system that renders rooms on the 3D map — drawing their walls, fills, and hover highlights — currently applies the same vivid blue hover fill regardless of whether the user is an editor working on a floor plan or a visitor exploring a published space. There is no concept of context: the layer just highlights whenever something is hovered.

Goal

Give the room layer a "view mode" setting so it can suppress the hover fill entirely in the editor, and switch to the new subtle colour in the preview, without changing anything for consumers that do not pass a mode.

What We're Building

A new optional setting on the room layer called view mode, which accepts one of three values: editor, preview, or map.

When view mode is set to editor, the layer never applies a fill highlight on hover, no matter which room the cursor is over. The room shapes stay visually neutral so the designer is not distracted while working.

When view mode is set to preview or map, the layer swaps the hover fill from the standard vivid blue to the subtle light blue-grey defined in Task 1 — the same quiet tone used by Mappedin. The fill appears only on named rooms (that logic lives in Task 5).

When no view mode is provided (the default), the layer behaves exactly as it does today, so nothing breaks for any component that has not yet been updated.

The switch also applies correctly when the map reloads its style or the user toggles between 2D and 3D view — the layer re-applies the right colour immediately rather than falling back to the default.

Why It Matters

Without this separation, every context gets the same hover treatment. That means a designer working carefully on room boundaries sees a distracting flash of blue every time the cursor passes over a room, and a preview visitor sees a louder highlight than the product's visual tone calls for. This task draws the line between those two contexts at the source — the layer renderer — so everything built on top of it inherits the correct behaviour automatically.

Acceptance Criteria

  • In editor mode, no fill colour appears on hovered rooms under any circumstances
  • In preview and map mode, hovered rooms show the subtle light blue-grey fill instead of the vivid blue
  • Components that do not pass a view mode see no change in behaviour
  • The paint correction applies after style reloads and 2D/3D mode switches — not just on initial load
  • The codebase builds, typechecks, and lints with zero new errors
  • The change is committed on its own

What Changes After This Task

The room layer understands modes. Task 4 (editor wiring) and Task 5 (preview wiring) will pass the correct mode to activate this behaviour in each context.

RESULT

Added viewMode: "editor" | "preview" | "map" to useFloorPlanLayer (src/lib/map/useFloorPlanLayer.ts): editor suppresses the hover highlight entirely; preview/map swap the vivid-blue fill for the subtle hover colour (Task 1) via a new applyHighlightPaint, re-applied after style reloads and 2D/3D switches. Adapted to the current applyHighlight(map, string[]) signature (editor passes []). The Map tab is wired to viewMode="map" so its hover fill uses the subtle colour too.

Commits: f4693da, 78027ea. Typecheck + ESLint clean. Merged to development (594af03).

issues.display_title: Issue #131: Teach the Label Canvas How to Behave Per Mode
issues.main_description_html:
Teach the Label Canvas How to Behave Per Mode

Docs

Spec

2026-06-22-hover-area-label-design.md

Plan

2026-06-22-hover-area-label.md

Context

The system that draws room name labels on the 3D map currently shows all labels at all times, regardless of whether the user is editing, previewing, or zoomed far out. In the editor this means every room's name is always on screen, which clutters the workspace. In the preview it means labels pile up when the map is zoomed out to show the whole building.

Goal

Give the label canvas a "view mode" setting so labels appear at the right time, in the right context, at the right scale — adapting automatically to whether the user is editing or exploring.

What We're Building

Three distinct label behaviours, selected by a new optional view mode setting:

Editor mode — Only the currently hovered room's label is drawn, and only if that room has a name. The label appears as the cursor moves over it and vanishes when the cursor leaves. No other labels are visible. This gives the designer a clean canvas to work on, with names available on demand rather than always in the way.

Preview and map mode (zoomed in) — All named room labels are drawn at once, spread across the floor plan with the existing declutter logic that prevents overlapping labels at high zoom levels. This is the existing behaviour, preserved for the zoomed-in experience.

Preview and map mode (zoomed out) — When the user zooms out past a set threshold (zoom level 17.5), individual room labels disappear and a single building name label appears at the geographical centre of the floor plan instead. This keeps the map readable at distance — one landmark label rather than a screen full of small text. Zooming back in restores the individual labels immediately.

The zoom threshold is tracked automatically via a listener — the canvas repaints as the user zooms, so the transition between building name and room labels is seamless.

When no view mode is provided, the canvas behaves exactly as it does today.

Why It Matters

Room labels are only useful in context. A designer mid-edit does not need all labels visible at once — they need to be able to glance at a room name without the screen being filled with text. A visitor zoomed out to see the whole building cannot read dozens of small labels overlapping at that scale — they need a single orientation anchor. This task gives each context exactly what it needs.

Acceptance Criteria

  • In editor mode, only the hovered room's label is visible; all other labels are hidden
  • In editor mode, rooms without a name show no label even when hovered
  • In preview/map mode at high zoom, all named room labels are shown with declutter (existing behaviour)
  • In preview/map mode when zoomed out past the threshold, individual labels disappear and the building name appears at the floor plan centre
  • Zooming back in past the threshold restores the individual room labels
  • The selected-room pin label (the teardrop pin beside a selected room) is not affected — it always renders in all modes
  • Components that do not pass a view mode see no change in behaviour
  • The codebase builds, typechecks, and lints with zero new errors
  • The change is committed on its own

What Changes After This Task

The label canvas understands modes and zoom. Task 4 (editor wiring) will activate editor-mode labels; Task 5 (preview wiring) will activate preview-mode labels and pass the building name.

RESULT

Added viewMode, hoveredAreaId, buildingName to useFloorPlanLabels (src/lib/map/useFloorPlanLabels.ts): editor = hovered room's label only; preview/map = all labels with declutter when zoomed in, single building-name label at the floor-plan centre below zoom 17.5 (tracked via a zoom listener). An undefined viewMode keeps the original behaviour (all labels always), so the Map tab is unaffected. The selected-room pin label and the point/safety marker draw are untouched.

issues.display_title: Issue #132: Connect the Editor to the New Mode System
issues.main_description_html:
Connect the Editor to the New Mode System

Docs

Spec

2026-06-22-hover-area-label-design.md

Plan

2026-06-22-hover-area-label.md

Context

Tasks 2 and 3 taught the room layer and the label canvas how to behave differently per view mode. But neither system knows yet that the editor exists — they are waiting to be told which mode to use. Until the editor passes "editor" as its view mode, both systems continue to behave as they always have.

Goal

Update the 3D map view inside the editor so it activates editor-mode behaviour in both the room layer and the label canvas.

What We're Building

Two small additions to the component that renders the 3D map in the editor:

  1. Room layer receives viewMode: "editor" — this tells the layer to suppress all hover fill highlights. Rooms will no longer flash blue when the cursor passes over them while the designer is working.

  2. Label canvas receives viewMode: "editor" and the ID of whichever room is currently hovered — this tells the canvas to show only that room's label on hover, and nothing otherwise.

The hovered room ID is already tracked by the editor's existing state — no new data fetching or store changes are needed. It just needs to be passed through to the label canvas alongside the mode.

Why It Matters

Without this wiring, the editor ignores all the mode-aware logic built in Tasks 2 and 3. The designer would still see vivid blue hover flashes and a screen full of room labels — the same behaviour as today. This task is the switch that turns the new behaviour on for the editing context.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Hovering a room in the editor no longer produces a fill highlight on the room extrusion
  • Hovering a named room in the editor shows that room's label
  • Hovering a room without a name shows nothing
  • Moving the cursor off a room makes the label disappear immediately
  • Area labels are not visible in the editor when nothing is hovered
  • Existing editor behaviours — room selection, pin labels, level switching — are unaffected
  • The codebase builds, typechecks, and lints with zero new errors
  • The change is committed on its own

What Changes After This Task

The editor operates in editor mode. The preview overlay is still in default mode — Task 5 will wire that separately.

RESULT

The map-hook editor wiring (originally on Editor3DMapView) was reverted per product feedback — the 3D Map tab keeps its original all-labels behaviour. Hover-only labels were instead implemented where the editor actually renders: the engine.

  • 2D canvas (draw.ts + interactions.ts): tracks the room/area polygon under the cursor (highlightRoom / hoverManual) and draws a room's name label only when hovered or selected; a small dot marks every room at all times.
  • 3D scene (scene3d.ts): room label sprites are tracked and their visibility gated the same way; recolor() toggles them, so hovering in either view reveals the matching label.

issues.display_title: Issue #133: Connect the Preview Overlay to the New Mode System
issues.main_description_html:
Connect the Preview Overlay to the New Mode System

Docs

Spec

2026-06-22-hover-area-label-design.md

Plan

2026-06-22-hover-area-label.md

Context

Tasks 2 and 3 built the mode-aware room layer and label canvas. Task 4 wired the editor. The preview overlay — the interactive 3D view that clients and stakeholders use to walk through a space before it is published — is still running in default mode and has not yet received its mode, its building name, or the name-gate logic that prevents hover highlights on unnamed rooms.

Goal

Update the preview overlay so it activates preview-mode behaviour: subtle hover fills on named rooms, a building name label when zoomed out, and no highlight response on rooms that have no name.

What We're Building

Three changes to the preview overlay component:

1. Room layer in preview mode — The layer receives viewMode: "preview", which activates the subtle light blue-grey fill (from Task 2) instead of the vivid blue. Rooms only light up when hovered; the selected-room blue remains unchanged.

2. Label canvas in preview mode with building name — The label canvas receives viewMode: "preview" and the building name pulled from the floor plan's information record. When the user zooms out past the threshold, the building name appears at the floor plan centre instead of the individual room labels. The building name is already available in the existing data — it just needs to be passed through.

3. Name-gate on hover — Currently, any room responds to hover regardless of whether it has a name. This change adds a check: before registering a hover, the system reads the room's name from the map data. If the name is empty or missing, no hover state is set — the room does not light up and no cursor change occurs. Only named rooms are interactive.

This name-gate matters because the preview is the product surface that external users see. Hovering an unnamed room and seeing nothing happen would feel broken. Silently ignoring unnamed rooms makes the interaction clean and intentional.

Why It Matters

The preview is the face of the product for visitors and clients. Vivid blue highlights feel like a debugging tool, not a polished product. Unnamed rooms responding to hover creates a confusing dead-end experience. Zoom-level label density is unreadable at scale. This task closes all three gaps, making the preview feel intentional and spatially aware.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Hovering a named room in the preview shows the subtle light blue-grey fill — not the vivid blue
  • Hovering a room without a name produces no fill and no visual response
  • Zooming out past the threshold hides individual room labels and shows the building name at the floor plan centre
  • Zooming back in restores the individual room labels
  • The selected-room highlight (distinct blue fill on a clicked room) is not affected
  • The selected-room pin label still renders correctly at all zoom levels
  • The label declutter logic (no overlapping labels at high zoom) still works
  • The codebase builds, typechecks, and lints with zero new errors
  • The change is committed on its own

What Changes After This Task

All five implementation tasks are complete. The editor and preview each have their own fully separate visual register. The public map viewer, when built, can opt into viewMode: "map" using the same pattern — no further infrastructure changes needed.

RESULT

Wired PreviewOverlay (src/components/editor/PreviewOverlay.tsx): viewMode="preview" on both hooks for the subtle hover fill and zoom-adaptive labels, buildingName from the first Information record, and a name-gate on the mousemove handler so unnamed areas produce no hover response.

issues.display_title: Issue #175: Floormap image not updating in editor after change
issues.main_description_html:
Floormap image not updating in editor after change

Bug

In the Edit Level modal, changing a level's floormap image did not update the editor's 2D plan backdrop until a full page reload.

Root cause

The freshly uploaded image 404s for a short window on the file endpoint (read-after-write lag). setBackdrop loaded the image once, hit the 404, and blanked the backdrop with no retry. A reload later fetched the same (now-servable) file successfully.

Fix

setBackdrop retries the image load up to 4x at 500ms with a cache-busted URL before falling back, and tracks the latest requested URL (ctx.bgUrl) so a stale retry can't overwrite the backdrop after a level switch.

Acceptance

  • Change a level's floormap image → editor backdrop updates within ~0.5-2s, no reload.
  • Switching levels mid-retry does not clobber the new level's backdrop.
  • Genuinely missing images still fall back to blank.

RESULT

Fixed in src/lib/newEditor/editor/model-sync.ts (setBackdrop retry + cache-bust), with ctx.bgUrl guard added in context.ts / index.ts. The backdrop now reloads the just-uploaded image through the transient 404 window, so the editor reflects the new floormap without a page reload. Typecheck + eslint pass.

Note: client-side mitigation for read-after-write lag on the file endpoint; the endpoint briefly 404ing after a successful upload is the underlying backend issue.

Delete unused floormap files on replace and level delete

issues.display_title: Issue #178: Edit Levels: view + remove image, close controls, tooltips
issues.main_description_html:
Edit Levels: view + remove image, close controls, tooltips

Add per-level actions in the Edit Levels modal:

  • View: fullscreen floormap preview (close via button, Esc, or backdrop).
  • Remove image: clears the level image and deletes the file (disk + record).
  • View/Remove shown only when the level has an image.
  • Tooltips (title) on every button.

Acceptance

  • View opens preview; closes on X / Esc / backdrop.
  • Remove clears image + deletes file (fire-and-forget).
  • Hovering any button shows a tooltip.

RESULT

Implemented in src/components/editor/EditLevelModal.tsx (View/Remove buttons, lightbox with X/Esc/backdrop close, titles on all buttons). Typecheck + eslint pass.

Commit: dfab01c

issues.display_title: Issue #179: Level dropdown -> shadcn combobox
issues.main_description_html:
Level dropdown -> shadcn combobox

Replace the native <select> level picker in the editor sidebar with a searchable shadcn combobox (Popover + Command), check mark on the active level, width matching the trigger.

Acceptance

  • Sidebar level picker is a searchable combobox.
  • Selecting a level sets the active level and closes.
  • Active level shows a check.

RESULT

src/components/editor/EditorPanel.tsx: added LevelCombobox (Popover + Command) replacing the <select>. Typecheck + eslint pass.

Commit: 29213fd

issues.display_title: Issue #180: Edit Project Info: real map + rename
issues.main_description_html:
Edit Project Info: real map + rename

Changes

  • Replace the map placeholder in the Edit File/Project Info modal with an actual MapViewer (same component as the wizard location step).
  • Centered crosshair pin for both modes: drag to move, fly-to on typed coords.
  • Save persists the dragged/typed coordinates in both Location and Lat-Lng modes.
  • Rename modal to "Edit Project Info" and label to "Project Name".

Acceptance

  • Map renders and is interactive; pin stays centered while dragging.
  • Typing coords flies the map to that point.
  • Saving stores the coords shown on the map.
  • Modal reads "Edit Project Info" / "Project Name".

RESULT

src/components/editor/EditFileModal.tsx: embedded MapViewer (crosshair, drag/fly-to), save uses map coords in both modes, renamed to Edit Project Info / Project Name. Typecheck + eslint pass.

Commit: b4e650d
